title: AI Implementation: A Practical Guide to Pilots, Risk, and Adoption
description: How to select an AI use case, evaluate outputs, protect data, measure value, and roll out AI with human oversight.
author: PilotStack Team

sections.title: Choose a bounded use case
sections.body: Start with a repeated task where the input, expected output, and cost of an error can be described. Examples include drafting a first version of an internal summary, classifying support requests for human review, or finding information in an approved knowledge base. Avoid beginning with an open-ended goal such as 'add AI everywhere.' Record the current process, time spent, failure rate, and the human decision that must remain accountable. Exclude sensitive or regulated data until the legal, security, and vendor terms have been reviewed.

sections.title: Create an evaluation set
sections.body: Before choosing a model or vendor, assemble representative examples that reflect routine work, edge cases, ambiguous requests, and known failure modes. Have qualified reviewers define what a correct, useful, and unsafe answer looks like. Score factual accuracy, completeness, consistency, latency, and the amount of editing required. Repeat the same evaluation when changing model versions or prompts. A handful of impressive demonstrations is not enough to estimate performance in everyday use.

sections.title: Review data and security boundaries
sections.body: Map which data is sent to the service, who can access prompts and outputs, how long records are retained, and whether submitted data may be used for model training. Confirm account-level controls, logging, deletion, regional requirements, and vendor subprocessors. Apply least-privilege access and do not paste credentials, customer secrets, or confidential records into an unapproved tool. For retrieval-based systems, test whether users can retrieve information they are not authorized to see.

sections.title: Keep humans in the right decisions
sections.body: Assign a named reviewer for consequential outputs and define when the system must abstain or escalate. Treat generated content as a proposal, not as evidence. Require source links for research tasks, validate calculations in deterministic tools, and prevent autonomous external actions until permissions and recovery paths have been tested. Give users a simple way to flag wrong answers and capture the correction so evaluation data improves over time.

sections.title: Pilot against a baseline
sections.body: Run the pilot with a small group and compare it with the existing workflow. Measure accepted output rate, correction time, error severity, latency, cost per completed task, and user confidence. Track cases where the model makes a plausible but incorrect claim separately from obvious failures. Set thresholds in advance for expanding, changing, or stopping the experiment. Include operational costs such as prompt maintenance, monitoring, review, and support rather than counting only API usage.

sections.title: Plan integration and ownership
sections.body: Decide where the tool fits in the workflow, how users authenticate, which systems it can read or change, and who handles outages or vendor changes. Start with read-only or draft-only access where possible. Version prompts, evaluation sets, and model settings; maintain a rollback path to the prior workflow. Train users on limitations and data handling, and make the approved use cases easy to find.

sections.title: Review value after launch
sections.body: After 30, 60, and 90 days, compare actual results with the original baseline. Look for changes in quality and downstream rework, not just number of prompts or generated words. Re-check access controls, retention settings, cost, and model behavior after product updates. Scale only when the use case remains valuable, the failure modes are understood, and the organization can support it. If the measured benefit does not justify the full cost and risk, narrow or retire the implementation.
